question.problem:
A fisherman catches fish continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $1$ fish every $15$ minutes. If the fisherman has already been fishing for $30$ minutes without catching any fish, what is the probability that he will need to fish for at least $20$ more minutes before catching his first fish? Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**

The required probability is
{{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
Since catching fish occurs continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next catch using an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the time until the next catch, in minutes. Since the fisherman catches $1$ fish every $15$ minutes on average, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{15}$ fish per minute, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{15}).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. So, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =\frac{1}{15},$ $s=30,$ and $t=20.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>30+20\,|\,X>30) & =P(X>20) \\  & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(1/15)\cdot (20)} \\  & ={e}^{-4/3} \\  & ≈0.264.\end{aligned}
$$
